Equally at paragraph 301 of the Strugar appeals judgement, the Appeals Chamber stressed, in the context of discussion of Article 7(3) liability, that a superior's failure to punish a crime of which he has actual knowledge is likely to be understood by his subordinates, at least, as acceptance, if not encouragement, of such conduct, with the effect of increasing the risk of new crimes being committed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. So in the circumstance of this case, Perisic's persistent failure to prevent or punish his subordinate's crimes perpetuated the environment of impunity which he inherited. This environment had a positive impact on his subordinates' actions and a substantial effect on their commissions of crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. Your Honours, I now turn to my submissions on Article 7(3), and I'll be making two brief submissions. Firstly, regarding the existence of a superior-subordinate relationship and secondly regarding the mens rea required for 7(3). As regards the existence of a superior-subordinate relationship, the Defence brief asserts at paragraph 72 that: "It must be proven that through his role or position, a personal relationship of subordination, vis-a-vis the perpetrators, was established and was acknowledged by both parties to that relationship." This, Your Honours, is legally incorrect. A superior-subordinate relationship arises where a superior has effective control over the subordinate, being the material ability to prevent or punish the subordinate's acts. As repeatedly affirmed, indicators of effective control are more a matter of evidence than of substantive law. An acknowledgement by a subordinate of a relationship of subordination may be a factual indicator of effective control, but it is not a prerequisite for finding a superior-subordinate relationship. Turning to the mens rea requirement for Article 7(3). Under Article -- under Article 7(3) liability, it must be shown that Perisic had knowledge or reason to know that crimes had been or were to be committed by his subordinates. On the Strugar appeals judgement at paragraphs 302 and 304 states that this standard is met if Perisic possessed sufficiently alarming information, putting him on notice of the risk that crimes might subsequently be carried out by his subordinates and justifying further inquiry. In discussing the requisite mens rea, the Defence misstates the law. In paragraphs 82 and 91 of the Defence brief, a number of tests are put forward citing ICTY and ICTR trial chamber jurisprudence and Bosnian state court jurisprudence in support. These tests suggest a higher mens rea standard. For example, at paragraph 82 of the Defence brief, the Defence states that there must be information putting a superior on notice of a present and real risk or likelihood of a legal act by his subordinates. The tests cited by the Defence are incorrect. If Perisic possessed information sufficiently alarming, putting him on notice of the risk that crimes might be subsequently carried out by his subordinates and justifying further inquiry, he had the requisite mens rea for liability under Article 7(3). The Defence brief at paragraph 83 states that knowledge of the commission of crimes generally is not sufficient. This point merits clarification. Paragraph 155 of the Krnojelac appeals judgement is authority for the proposition that, with regard to a specific offence, for example, murder, the information available to the superior need not contain specific details on the unlawful acts which have been or are about to be committed. Rather, the information must provide general notice of the type of crimes charged. At paragraph 83 of the Defence brief, the Defence cites the Oric appeals judgement at paragraph 59 of the Oric appeals judgement, which states that knowledge of a crime and knowledge of a person's criminal conduct are, in law and in fact, distinct matters. This is correct. But the Oric appeals judgement in the same paragraph goes on to say that the latter may be inferred from the former. So as with the mens rea standard for Article 7(1), Perisic need not have had notice of the precise scheduled incidents. Rather the Prosecution must prove that Perisic had notice of the attacks on civilians, the murder, and the inhumane acts being committed by his subordinates as part of the campaign of shelling and sniping in Sarajevo, and equally, the Prosecution must prove that he had had notice of the murders, extermination, inhumane acts and persecutions committed by his subordinates in Srebrenica. Your Honours, unless you have any further questions on the applicable law, I will turn to my submissions on the personnel centres. As Mr. Harmon outlined, Perisic aided and abetted the crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica by the provision of assistance which had a substantial effect on those crimes. The first element of the assistance provided by Perisic was personnel through the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres. I'll be making three main submissions in respect of the personnel centres. Firstly that the personnel centres addressed an essential need of the VRS. Secondly, that the VJ remained the ultimate arbiter of whether an individual returned to the FRY from the VRS or the SVK. And thirdly, that the regulation of status provided by the personnel centres was vitally important. Turning to my first submission. The personnel centres addressed an essential need of the VRS. Prior to the creation of the personnel centres, the provision of VJ officers to the VRS and the SVK was ad hoc and unregulated. This created serious problems for those armies. It resulted in a drain of personnel giving rise to both damage to combat readiness and damage to combat morale. And these problems were set out in detail in a March 1993 request from Mladic to the to the then VJ Chief of General Staff, Perisic's predecessor, regarding the prevention of personnel from leaving the VRS. And that's P1529 that Your Honours will see on the screen before you. And Your Honours, I intend to go through this letter in some detail. In this letter, Mladic highlighted that a large number of VRS personnel were abandoning their units without permission to leave for the VJ, and at this point I'll just note that there is a revised translation of this document which the Defence have agreed, and I'll just point out the revised wording. The revised -- the Prosecution will be making a written submission on this but the revised wording will read that "a large number of active military personnel and army employees abandoned their units without permission and leave for the Yugoslav Army." Mladic went on to emphasise that: "The damage stemming from this to combat readiness, especially combat morale in the Army of Republika Srpska is multifaceted. A large number of officers in command posts with high responsibility leave units without handing over their duties, because of which units suffer losses or their tactical position is jeopardised along the front line; troops remain uncared for and left to their own devices; units remain without officers for an extended period; and the negative influence on morale is extremely harmful since active officers are involved." Mladic proceeded: "Based on the above and in order to overcome negative consequences and maintain the necessary level of combat readiness in the units of the Army of Republika Srpska, please take the necessary measures in your authority to put a stop to the unauthorised return to the Yugoslav Army of active military personnel and civilian employees who are engaged in the Army of Republika Srpska ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we say that letter is dated the 31st of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: 1993. Mladic emphasised the necessity of VRS agreement prior to the return of those officers stating: "Every individual request to return to the VJ will be reviewed by the relevant commands and officers of the VRS, who will issue the appropriate agreement. Among other things, your measures are necessary to prevent the admission and assignment and especially promotion of all those who return without this agreement." Mladic went on to underline the VRS's continuing need for additional personnel, stating: "Please adopt an enactment making it obligatory for all active military personnel who come from the former Bosnia-Herzegovina to join the Army of Republika Srpska at the request of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska ... "All those who refuse to comply with this request must be removed from the Yugoslav Army in an appropriate procedure." On this last point he urged the termination of those who refused to go, stating: "If they are not prepared to defend their own homeland, they will not want to fight for someone else's." Finally, Mladic highlighted the unequal treatment of personnel serving in the VRS in housing and status matters and requested that subordinated commands be prevented from adopting enactments with negative status decisions for active military personnel who are engaged in the Army of Republika Srpska while they are with us."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, Your Honour. Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the appropriate time for you, you have a minute or two still. If you are going to another point, we can stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm moving on to another point, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, before the break we had done a detailed review of P1529 which was Mladic's letter from March 1993 highlighting the problems which the VRS had at that point. When Perisic became VJ Chief of General Staff some five months later these problems remained unresolved. Indeed the issues highlighted by Mladic in that letter are precisely those which were emphasised by Perisic both in his written submission to the SDC on the formation of the personnel centres and his discussions in his discussions with the SDC on the personnel centres. In the next series of slides, we'll do a comparison between the issues as highlighted by Mladic and as addressed by Perisic in these discussions. Turning to the first issue, Mladic had highlighted the problem of morale in the VRS, and again, Your Honours will recognise this text as the text that we had previously reviewed before the break. On the topic of morale, Perisic in his written submissions before the SDC, and that's P1872, document ID 0630-6544, stated that: "Considering the fact that VJ officers born in Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia who did not respond to the VRS are or SVK call-up, "were better provided for in everything regarding service, housing, and so on in relation to the active servicemen who stayed behind or were subsequently dispatched, we must accept that there is a reason for constant misunderstandings, various requests, and moral dilemmas with reference to these active servicemen and problems regarding their actual obligations based on the service in the VJ." Secondly, Mladic had urged of additional officers born in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the VRS requesting than an enactment be adopted making it obligatory for those personnel to join the VRS at the request of the VRS Main Staff or be terminated from the VJ. Again, in Perisic's written submission on this topic, Perisic echoes or, rather, responds to this need. The submission states that: "In the proposed order of the FRY president to be put into effect by the VJ Chief of General Staff, all professional soldiers and civilians serving in the VJ who were born in Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina and sent to do their training or service in the JNA from these territories, would be obliged to respond to call-up from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska or the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or else their service in the Yugoslav Army would be terminated." On this issue of termination, Mladic's position had been very clear stating that if they were not prepared to defend their own homeland, they would not be -- they would not want to fight for someone else's. This stated position by Mladic resonates throughout Perisic's statements on this topic to the SDC. At the 14th SDC session on the 11th of October, 1993, Perisic stated: "If those men refuse to go there, then we need to view them as deserters who don't want to defend their homes." That's at page 33 of P709. Later in the same session at page 36 of the exhibit, Perisic stated: "If such an individual is not ready to go fight anywhere, and this is a single people, we need to think about whether he should be in this army at all." And then at the next SDC session, the 15th session, on the 10th of November, 1993, this is P780, page 5, Perisic states: "If someone flatly refuses to go, then I'll do everything I can to help him leave the army, because, if he doesn't want to defend his people when they are most threatened, when will he defend them?" Mladic had also highlighted the problem of unequal regulation of status of officers serving in the VRS, and requested that an enactment be made regularising that service. Again, Perisic made repeated submissions on this issue to the SDC. With reference to those VJ officers serving in the VRS and the SVK, he stated, and this is in his written submission at P1872: "The legal position and personal status of all those persons (those who stayed behind and those who were dispatched there) has not been equally regulated, regarding salary, promotion in rank and service, provision of care for the families in the FRY, right to provision of housing, and other service rights." Before the 14th session of the SDC, Perisic stated, at page 32 of P709: "In order to have a foothold, we have paved the way for the president of the state, in his capacity as supreme commander, to issue an order regulating their status and that of officers here." And later that same session he emphasised that: "I'm insisting that they should get the same status as officers here." Finally, Mladic's 1993 letter had highlighted the problem of the return of officers to the VJ without VRS consent, and the impact that the drain of officers was having on VRS combat readiness and combat morale and the need for VRS consent to be mandatory prior to an officer's return. To that end, the instructions on the personnel centres signed by Perisic provided for the consent of the personnel centre commander prior to the return of an officer to the VJ. These instructions are at P734 and the relevant page is page 7 and the relevant provision provides that: "In keeping with service requirements, professional soldiers and civilian personnel sent or transferred to the personnel centre may be returned, assigned, or transferred to the VJ units or institutions with the consent or on the recommendation of the personnel centre Main Staff." This provision ensured that the needs of service of the VRS and the SVK would be considered, that the drain of personnel would be prevented, and that the army's combat readiness would be protected. The Defence gives an incomplete and inaccurate account of Starcevic's testimony on this particular provision of the instructions. Paragraph 264 of the Defence brief cites a direct Starcevic quote, and I quote that: "If this paragraph stipulates that they can return to the VJ, at this point in time, they must not have been in the VJ, since this paragraph provides for their return. There is no other reasonable or legal understanding of this term." In fact, in an exchange beginning at T-6924, line 4 of the transcript, Defence counsel had asked Mr. Starcevic: "If this paragraph stipulates that they can return to the VJ, am I right in understanding it, that at this point they were not in the VJ, since this paragraph provides for their return?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STARCEVIC RESPONDED
utterances.text: "To put it simply, there is no other reasonable or legal understanding of this item. But if you view this paragraph separate from everything else that we have seen." Mr. Starcevic then went on to elaborate at T-6925, line 2 of the transcript that: "The counsel has offered an interpretation for which I said there could be no other reasonable or legal understanding of this item. But, if we perceive this item separate from other provisions that we have seen before, but only if we perceive this item separate."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does that mean? I don't understand that last quotation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this means that this document, in common with the other documents with which the Trial Chamber has before it, cannot be viewed in isolation, but and as Mr. Harmon will discuss further in his submissions on Article 7(3), Mr. Starcevic testified that the personnel centres were members of the VJ as a matter of law [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: In summary, the personnel centres proposed by Perisic addressed the needs highlighted by Mladic by formalizing the support being provided by the VJ to the VRS and the SVK by, firstly, creating a mechanism to staunch the flow of personnel from those armies by ensuring that the VRS and SVK commanders could act as gatekeepers, preventing the unauthorised return of officers to the FRY. Secondly, by ensuring that the rights of those officers serving in VRS and the SVK would be fully protected and enjoyed in the same manner and scope as those of other VJ members. And thirdly, by providing the VJ, in Perisic's words, with legal cover to ensure that it could continue to transfer officers to the VRS and SVK in order to maintain and support their war efforts. Perisic was the architect of the personnel system through which the VRS and the SVK commands were provided the security of knowing that the VJ would continue to support them by providing further officers, preventing a personnel drain, and thereby ensuring that the command structure remain solid. And the officers themselves were given the security of knowing that their livelihoods would be protected, and together this ensured that the combat readiness and the combat morale of the VRS and SVK would be sustained. Turning to my second submission. Throughout this period, however, the VJ remained the ultimate arbiter of whether an individual returned to the FRY from the VRS or the SVK. The Defence brief at paragraph 304 states that requests from officers in the VRS and the SVK to rejoin the VJ were decided by the VRS and SVK commander and that Perisic played no role in the decision, nor is there any evidence that he was able to overrule and influence any decision in other armies. The purpose of the personnel centres was to sustain and maintain the VRS and SVK officer corps and for this reason, as we have seen, the instructions on the personnel centres provided for VRS or SVK consent prior to the return of officers to the FRY. The Prosecution doesn't dispute that the VRS and the SVK made the majority of decisions as to assignment to duty within those armies, and that the duties to which officers were assigned in the personnel centres reflected the decisions that had been made by the VRS and the SVK commands. And that's set out in paragraphs 176 and 183 of the Prosecution brief. And Your Honours, this is consistent with the purpose of the personnel centres, namely, to supply officers in accordance with the VRS and SVK needs of service. However, it's clear from the documents in evidence that Perisic and the VJ retained the ultimate authority as to who could return to the FRY. Paragraph 193 of the Prosecution brief discusses P2864, which is a instruction from the VJ General Staff personnel administration to the 40th Personnel Centre Main Staff and it provides that -- dealing with the issue of officers transferring out of the 40th Personnel Centre, and the instruction provides that: "Recommendations for transfer from the 40th Personnel Centre may be submitted only through the 40th Personnel Centre Main Staff and with the 40th Personnel Centre Main Staff commander's signature. The transfer can be executed only after reception of response - approval from the VJ General Staff personnel administration." The examples cited by the Defence at paragraph 304 of its brief all relate to instances where an officer himself requested transfer. Given the VJ's purpose in supplying the officers to the VRS and the SVK - namely to support the war effort, it's unsurprising that the approval of those officers' immediate superior was standard before they came back to the VJ or to the FRY. Ultimately, however, the determination as to whether an officer stayed in the personnel centres or returned to the FRY rested with the VJ, and its needs of service overrode all others. D335 is a VRS Main Staff personnel sector response to an officer's request for transfer out of the 30th Personnel Centre. The officer is of informed that his case was discussed at the VRS Main Staff commander advisory board and that: "A decision was made to forward your request to the 30th Personnel Centre with a proposal to the officer in charge to issue an order for transfer to the VJ outside the 30th Personnel Centre." So the VRS considered the case and decided to propose to the VJ that the officer be transferred. The VJ remained the ultimate arbiter. Equally, paragraph 192 of the Prosecution brief discusses the case of VJ Major-General Branislav Petrovic, who had been deployed to serve in the 11th Corps in the Slavonia Baranja district. That's P2754. This case the Slavonia Baranja Corps chain of command requested to Perisic personally that Petrovic be permitted to stay in the Slavonia Baranja corps until after completion of the operations in the territory. The office of the VJ Chief of General Staff responded stating that Perisic -- that Petrovic was required to return to duty in the VJ General Staff air force administration and "his re-engagement in the defence of the Slavonia and Baranja district shall be duly regulated based on the indicators of the beginning of the aggression against this district." That is, the VJ refused the request to resend him, but informed the Slavonia Baranja Corps command that they would reconsider resending him in the event that there was aggression against it. So in summary, contrary to the Defence contention, the VJ remained the ultimate arbiter as to whether individuals returned to the FRY, and Perisic himself could overrule other armies' decisions. Turning to my third submission, regulation of status was vitally important. Proper record-keeping, necessary to regulate status and protect status rights, was an integral function of the personnel centres. That's acknowledged at paragraph 255 of the Defence brief and paragraph 200 and 201 of the Prosecution brief. As is evident from Mladic's 1993 request, this regulation was vitally important to the effective functioning of the armies. It reassured VJ officers and their families of their livelihood, giving them security in a chaotic time and providing them both with a financial life-line and moral support. And this enabled them to serve in the VRS and the SVK as part of the VJ assistance provided to the VRS and the SVK war effort. The Defence concedes in its brief that the regulation of status and the protection of status-related rights was necessary and important. The status-related rights regulated included those relating to salary, pension, housing, and promotions, and there is a wealth of evidence showing the importance of status-related rights to officers and their families as outlined at paragraphs 201 and 209 to 210 of the Prosecution brief. Defence witness Stamenko Nikolic testified that personal records in relation to members of the VJ were exceptionally important. It's important for regulating the position and status of a member within an army. He proceeded to testify regarding the failure to keep records of those former JNA members serving in the VRS and the SVK that those persons were facing such a situation that "unless their status was resolved and the rights they enjoyed under their status, this would have utterly destroyed their families and made their survival as human beings entirely impossible." Perisic understood the importance of status regulation and the salaries being received by the officers and in June 1994 at the 21st SDC session, that's P776, having set out the numbers of VJ officers serving in the VRS and SVK and the amounts that were allocated annually for their salaries, he stated, "that's a great help to them." In November 1994, following the FRY sanctions against the Republika Srpska, Mladic complained that stopping the salaries to VJ members serving in the VRS had caused "an enormous existential crisis for their families. A situation has been created in which the attention is necessarily drawn from combat tasks. Deferring of this issue is making the matters worse for the professional soldiers of the VJ and their families." And again Defence Nikolic testified in relation to resolving this problem that -- and witness Nikolic was dealing with the families at issue. He stated: "This agony went on for a full five months and I have never in my life faced a crisis as severe as that." Indeed, following the imposition of these sanctions, in September 1994, Perisic sent 500.000 dinars to Mladic for salaries for VJ officers serving in the VRS. And that's P851. Actions taken by officers, including Dragomir Milosevic and Mladic, to enforce their status-related rights including compensation for unused annual leave, injury compensation, separation allowance and unpaid salaries are discussed at length in paragraphs 788 to 799 of the Prosecution brief. One element of this status regulation was promotions. The Defence wrongly limits its analysis or its discussions of promotions in the VJ to a 7(3) context. However, promotions and their regulation were also a clear component of the assistance provided by Perisic under Article 7(1). The Defence argues that promotions of VJ officers serving in the VRS were made final in the VRS and that the only steps taken in the VJ were to verify those promotions to regulate the status rights of an officer. This is incorrect and Perisic's active role in this regard will be discussed by Mr. Harmon in the context of his submissions on Article 7(3). However, the Defence accepts at paragraph 383 of its brief that an officer's rank formed part of the basis of payment for increased salary and other attendant benefits, such as pension entitlements. The Defence also accepts at paragraph 415 to 420 of its brief, that any change in salary, pension contributions, housing priorities or other status-related rights only became effective when a VJ officer was promoted in the VJ. As with the other elements of status regulation, this was important to officers serving in the VRS. For example, in Galic's VRS exit interview at P1760 on the 12th of August, 1994, the first point that Galic made was: "Before the adoption of a decision on the termination of my professional military service, I wish my appointment to my current post of commander of the SRK establishment rank Lieutenant-General PG-4 rank group, to be verified." Promotions were also good for morale, and Perisic strongly advocated for promotions of VJ officers serving in the VRS and the SVK on that basis. At the 15th SDC session on the 10th of November, 1993, and that's P780, page 23, Perisic stated in relation to promotions: "We'll be giving them moral support. It's not just the matter of a flat or something like that. These men are fighting and by doing so, they are ensuring peace to us. I urge - and that's why I proposed - that they be given this since it would greatly motivate them. In doing so, we would recognise what they have done." In summary, Your Honours, the regulation of status-related rights relating to salary, pension, housing, and promotions, and the security of access to those rights, enabled VJ officers to serve in the VRS and the SVK for as long as they were so regulated. It gave the officers serving in the VRS the comfort to stay as long as they were needed in the knowledge that they weren't giving up their VJ benefits. No such security was available for former JNA officers serving in the ABiH or the HVO. Through sustaining and maintaining the VRS officer corps, the assistance provided through the personnel centres had a substantial effect on the crimes committed in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. That concludes my submissions on the personnel centres, Your Honours. Unless you have any further questions, I will hand over to my colleague Mr. Thomas. Excuse me, one moment, Your Honours. My apologies, Your Honours, Mr. Harmon has just pointed out an error in the transcript which is at page 62, line 16. And it currently states that personnel centres were members of the VJ as a matter of law. And it should of course read that persons serving in the personnel centres were members of the VJ as a matter of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Again, unless Your Honours have any questions, I will hand over to my colleague Mr. Thomas who will make submissions on the second element of the assistance provided by Mr. Perisic, namely the logistical and materiel assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the time left before we break, I will endeavour to discuss the aspects of the logistics case, namely the assistance provided by the VJ to the VRS in weapons, ammunition and other logistics assistance. In doing so, I don't propose to discuss the Prosecution case in any detail. I don't wish to summarise it in any way. The Prosecution allegations are substantiated by an analysis of the wealth of evidence that has been tendered in this case and which is described in our final trial brief. I don't -- we don't seek to augment that analysis or qualify that analysis in any way today. What I would like to do, Your Honours, however, is just to take the opportunity to address a number of misconceptions under which the Defence appear to be operating when it comes to this part of the case. The first of those is the interrelationship between the VJ and the FRY Ministry of Defence. The Defence have made the assertion that in the budget planning and production phase, namely the phase during which funds are being made available for the VJ and production requirements are being assessed and paid for, the Defence have asserted that during this period, the VJ is operating or was operating under the authority of the MOD, the FRY MOD, and that assertion, Your Honours, is found at paragraph 613 of the Defence final trial brief. That misstates the true relationship between the VJ and the FRY Ministry of Defence. At the time that General Perisic took his position as Chief of the General Staff, there had been the restructure of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence and as a result of that restructure, the VJ and the FRY MOD were each -- sorry, neither the VJ nor the MOD were subordinated to the other. In practical terms, what that meant was that the FRY MOD had the responsibility for submitting a national defence budget to the FRY Assembly. For the purposes of that national defence budget, let me go back a step Your Honours. The national defence budget provided for the VJ requirements and it provided for the FRY MOD requirements. In other words, funds were put aside for the functioning of both the VJ and the functioning of the MOD in the national defence budget. By far, the larger component of the national defence budget was to meet VJ needs. Although the MOD was responsible for preparing the draft national defence budget, because the vast proportion of the VJ national budget went to providing for VJ needs, it would seek from the VJ General Staff a draft VJ budget plan. The VJ would essentially provide a submission to the FRY MOD seeking funds for its operations. That was prepared by the General Staff of the VJ. In it, they would seek funds for the coming year for all of their needs. The single biggest need was salary, or the single biggest need during the indictment period was the payment of salaries. And incorporated in that request for funds for salaries from the VJ included the amounts that were payable to VJ officers serving in the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres. Also sought by the VJ General Staff in its budget plans would be the other requirements or other needs for it to properly function, including the replenishments of its reserves. Once the VJ General Staff had prepared that budget plan and it was forwarded to the FRY Ministry of Defence, we've heard evidence that there would, on occasion, be discussion as to whether or not that VJ budget plan was realistic, in other words, whether given the state of the FRY at that time that the FRY Assembly would likely pass a budget that contained such requests or whether the VJ budget plan would need to be amended to make it a little more realistic in that respect. However, ultimately, the two entities reached a position where the VJ budget plan for the coming year had been submitted by the General Staff to the MOD. The MOD incorporated it in the draft national defence budget, which was then sent for approval to the FRY Assembly. Once the FRY Assembly approved the budget, the MOD was responsible for disbursing funds against that budget in large measure. In particular, the MOD was responsible for disbursing the individual salaries to the individual officers concerned, but, of course, this was against the funds put aside for that purpose in the national defence budget as requested by the General Staff. The FRY MOD was also responsible for ensuring that the funds that had been approved for the replenishment of VJ reserves were put to that purpose, and in practical terms that meant that the FRY MOD would arrange for the necessary production from the special-purpose industry facilities that Your Honours have heard about during the course of this trial. And those special-purpose industries being subordinated to the Ministry of Defence would produce the necessary material, and upon production of that material, it would be sent to the VJ to replenish VJ reserves. Now, the evidence on all of that comes from two Defence witness, General Stamenko Nikolic, who was the FRY MOD head of administration for systems and status-related administration affairs, and General Jovanic, who was FRY MOD head of finance and budget administration. General Nikolic also provided Your Honours a piece of evidence that corroborates other evidence in this trial, but which is important when it comes to the logistics case, because notwithstanding that relationship between the VJ and the MOD, once material that had been produced by FRY special-purpose industry formed part of VJ reserves, it came under the control of General Perisic. It was General Perisic as Chief of the General Staff who had authority to decide the use to which the VJ reserves would be put. And it's important, Your Honours, when we look at P1009, which we could have on the screen for a moment, to view the document in that context and Your Honours will recall this document from Mr. Harmon's presentation and also from the occasions that we have seen it during the course of this trial. This is the order where the -- this is the order where President Lilic authorises the Yugoslav Army - not the MOD, but the Yugoslav Army - to supply the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres with weapons and military equipment. And this is where President Lilic authorises General Perisic to regulate the requests submitted to the VJ by the VRS and the SVK with the means of the VJ to fulfill those requests from the reserves which he had authority over. This order exists, Your Honour, because General Perisic asked for it. General Perisic knew full well his legal obligations and the state of the law when it came to disbursing military equipment. He understood that he had no right to send military equipment, weapons and ammunition, to another army. He understood that the materiel wasn't his to give in the first place, because ownership of it vested in the Ministry of Defence. Nevertheless, it was he who advocated for the issue of this order, so that the Yugoslav Army could provide this materiel to the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres, and so that he could control that process. This comes from the 18th session of the Supreme Defence Council. At a session on the 7th of February, 1994, which preceded by a matter of days the order being issued by President Lilic, and if we can move, please, to the first highlighted section. Thank you. And this is General Perisic, Your Honours, addressing the members of the SDC. They are discussing the provision of assistance to the SVK and the VRS or the specifically the provision of VJ assistance to the VRS and the SVK. He states: "The property law which entered into force does not give the Chief of General Staff any right to misappropriate any resource, especially in terms of assistance and specifically now to Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we put a [sic] after misappropriation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can we move to the second part of the quote please. "Either things should remain the way they are regulated by law," in other words I can't send it, "or the supreme council should adopt the decision to authorise me to give them something that this body decides upon. So they make a request to the supreme council, I convey it to you and say whether this is justified or not. You make a decision and then it is implemented by the Chief of the General Staff. This is the way I propose because we really have to bear this in mind. If the two Krajinas are not defended, we will be significantly jeopardised and they certainly can't be defended without our assistance and weapons and military equipment." So as I've said, Your Honour, the result of that submission by General Perisic so the SDC on the 7th of February was for President Lilic to issue the order that we have just been looking at, ordering the VJ to provide weapons and ammunition to the VRS and SVK, and also authorising General Perisic to reconcile the requests. In other words, to say whether this is justified or not as he has pleaded before the SDC on the 7th of February. The second misapprehension that I'd like to address is related to the first, namely the relationship between the VJ and the MOD. In a part of its final trial brief entitled, "VRS knowledge" -- sorry, "VRS understanding of request process," and this is at paragraph 633 of the Defence final trial brief, the Defence quote General Dusan Kovacevic. General Kovacevic testified that if the VRS needed anything, the VRS would go to the RS Ministry of Defence. The RS Ministry of Defence would go in turn to either its own special purpose abilities or to the FRY MOD, not to the VJ but to the FRY MOD, to source what had been requested by the VRS. If the FRY MOD were not able to provide what the RS MOD was seeking, then President Karadzic would go to see Slobodan Milosevic and see if Mr. Milosevic could find a way to provide what was needed. Now, what is patently missing from that description of the process is what actually occurred. General Kovacevic was the minister of defence for the Republika Srpska at that time and what he was testifying about was the role that the FRY MOD had in securing materiel for the needs of the VRS. But what his testimony fails to take into account is the reality of the situation which was that, in furtherance to the order that we've seen from President Lilic, General Perisic established a system whereby requests would go direct from the Main Staff of the VRS to the General Staff of the VJ. We've had plenty of testimony on that during this trial and there are plenty exhibits showing that process and operation. Mladic or somebody else from the VRS Main Staff would send a request to the General Staff. It would find its way to General Perisic, he would direct that the request be forwarded to the appropriate logistics organ for an opinion as to whether or not the materiel could be supplied. If the materiel could be supplied, then General Perisic or his cabinet would issue an order to that effect and the materiel would be supplied. This was a process that bypassed both the RS MOD and the FRY MOD. It was nothing to do with the MOD. This was Perisic carrying out Lilic's order, the order obtained at his request to directly supply, VJ to VRS, the 30th Personnel Centre with weapons and ammunition, to regulate the requests and to provide an opinion based on the ability of the VJ to meet those requests, and to provide that assistance to the extent that the VJ could meet those requests. The next misapprehension I'd like to discuss, Your Honours, is a submission by the Defence that it was the Serbian MUP who controlled official border crossings. And that submission is made at paragraph 681 of the Defence final trial brief. First of all, the Prosecution accepts that official border crossings were under the control of the police, the Serbian MUP. However, official border crossings were only part of the picture and the reality was that unofficial border crossings played as much a role, if not more, in the provision of assistance than anything else. First of all, it was General Vuksic, the VJ General Staff assistant chief of relations with foreign armies who explained the difference between MUP control of border crossings and VJ control of the border. And if we could move to his testimony. He was asked by my learned friends for the Defence: " Why was the VJ not in a position to control in full the so-called border?" And his answer was: "If we are talking about borders in the standard meaning of the term, the military never controlled the entire border-line, only the stretches between official border crossings. At the official border crossings, there was the police as well as customs." And this becomes important testimony when one considers, Your Honours, that the official border crossings were bypassed and they were bypassed deliberately, which means that supplies were going through the parts of the border that were controlled by the VJ. Could we go -- I am sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand what you are saying, read with what has been said here and I just want you to clarify this. If we are talking about borders in the standard meaning of the term, the military never controlled the entire border-line, "only the stretches between official border crossings." What does that last phrase mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The VJ controlled the entire border-line, was responsible for controlling the entire border-line, Your Honour, with the exception of official crossing points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: So the official crossing points would have police and customs but the rest of the border was the responsibility of the VJ. And as I've said, Your Honour, this becomes important when one considers that effectively unofficial crossings were used. And if we could move very briefly, Your Honours, into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are we are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further support for that proposition comes from General Djukic, Your Honour, who was the VRS deputy chief for logistics and I'm reading now from his 92 quater statement: "I know that the transfer of the weapon and ammunition was carried out secretly," in the areas stated, "by civilian trucks avoiding border crossings where there were UNPROFOR observers." So while it might be true, Your Honours, that the Serbian MUP and customs and UNPROFOR observers were present at official border crossings, there are, as you can see, self-evident reasons why unofficial crossings were used to transport this material. The next matter that I'd like to briefly address, Your Honour, is again similarly related to this concept of VJ versus MOD. At paragraph 718 of the Defence final trial brief, the Defence accept that there is evidence showing that certain entities provided materiel to the VRS and they list three. They list Kragujevac, they list the depot at Mrsac and they list Krusik factory and Valjevo. They assert in their paragraph that these three entities, however, were not VJ entities or subordinated to the VJ. However, in this respect they are wrong, both Kragujevac and Mrsac were, in fact, VJ entities and a concession more appropriately that these two as VJ entities sent weapons and ammunition to the VRS and that Krusik as an MOD entity sent materiel. The authority for that proposition first of all, comes from General Kodzopeljic who was in charge of Kragujevac. He was the VJ General Staff chief of technical administration. And he was asked specifically about the status or the subordination of the Kragujevac Technical Institute. If we could move to that testimony, please. Starting about halfway down that quote, Your Honours: "What I'd like you to do if you could, is I'd like you to explain to us the technical institutes and how the Military Technical Institutes and specifically the Military Technical Institutes with regard to repair, fit into your duties, if you could." And his answer: "I can only speak of the technical and maintenance institutes that were under me." In other words as chief of the technical administration of the VJ General Staff. "It was the institute in Kragujevac and Cacak." MP-14 testified about the subordination of the Mrsac military depot to Kragujevac, thereby establishing its status at a VJ military unit. In discussing a particular materiel list, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Earlier you asked to go into private session where you discussed this witness, are you happy to do so now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, this was testimony given in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In discussing a particular materiel list, MP-14 stated that "Kragujevac is the sender and the place, Mrsac, that's probably a depot somewhere in Serbia. I wouldn't know where it was. And it belonged to the main military post in Kragujevac. Just as the 27th base was my main military post and Kragujevac was subordinate to it, so the main command would be at Kragujevac and the depot would be in Mrsac." Placing both of those, Your Honour, under the authority of the VJ General Staff chief of technical administration, General Kodzopeljic. Further support for the status of Mrsac comes from a document, several, but this is one of several which will suit our purposes. This is an order issued by the 1st Army of the VJ, in July 1994. "Further to a decision," so this is, first of all, Your Honours, it's important to note that this is a VJ order. "Further to decision confidential number 85-35, dated 21 April 1994, issued by the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, issued to the 30th Personnel Centre, the following types and quantities of ammunition from herein below listed military posts." And amongst those listed we have military post 5292, Mrsac, 7.9 millimetre bullet, 1 million rounds; 7.62 millimetre bullet, 750.000 rounds. So from those pieces of evidence, Your Honour, you have established, as well as from others, that the Defence concession that these entities provided materiel to the VRS is a concession that these VJ installations provided the materiel. The final matter I'd like to very briefly address, Your Honours, is one that was the subject of much discussion by my learned friends in the Defence final trial brief and that is General Mladic's report to the 50th Bosnian Serb Assembly session on the 15th of April, 1995. And this is discussed from paragraph 732 onwards in the Defence final trial brief. At this Bosnian Serb Assembly session, General Mladic was invited to address the delegates on the state of the war, the state of the VRS, its activities, its combat readiness and its needs. And during the course of that address, he described materiel that had been used, that had been consumed by the VRS from the very beginning of the war through until December 1994, and the various sources of that materiel. For example, he stated that the VJ had provided 47.2 per cent of infantry ammunition consumed by the VRS in that period, and he gave other percentages of other items. However, Your Honours, it's important to not look at this document in isolation. This is a theme that has been picked up by others who have gone before me. First of all, well, not least of all, the time-period referred to by General Mladic was from the beginning of the war in Bosnia through to December 1994, in other words, it includes a large period that preceded General Perisic as Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, and significantly in that period, as we've seen from documents referred to by Mr. Harmon, it was during this early period that the VRS had the benefit of being able to rely very heavily on reserves left behind by the retreating JNA. The point is, the document is useful only when it is placed up against the entire body of evidence that Your Honours have in relation to logistics. As I've said, that discussion appears more fully in our final trial brief. I can do no more at this point, Your Honours, than to simply state that we rely on the entire body of evidence and for the conclusions that Your Honours feel that you can draw from that entire body of evidence, but our position is that from the testimony and from the exhibits, it was clearly articulated FRY policy to assist the RS and the RSK. It was FRY policy for the VJ to directly supply the VRS and the SVK with weapons, ammunition, and other logistics assistance. Perisic was authorised to make sure that happened. He set in place procedures necessary to make that happen. He continued to involve himself in those procedures throughout his tenure. Throughout this time, the VJ did supply materiel to the VRS on repeated occasions and that throughout the indictment period, when the VRS had no more JNA reserves left, this assistance was crucial and substantial. Your Honours, those are my submissions. Unless you have any questions, I will leave it at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas. Yes, Mr. Harmon, who is next?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next submissions will be made by me. I see that we only have five minutes left for today's session, I'm happy to begin. However, clearly with as fast as I talk I still can't get my entire submission done in the five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Carter. I understand that to be saying we should take an early break.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm at the leave of the discretion of Your Honours. I'm happy to begin or happy to begin in the morning, whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break then and come back tomorrow. Court adjourned to tomorrow morning, 9.00. Same court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of March, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 25
